title: By the charcoal fire (John 18:12–27)
hook: Peter warms himself and denies him

segments.voice: Yesterday, torches in the garden, Malchus's ear cut off, and two words that knocked soldiers to the ground. Your line was I am he. Did you take the first step? Day six hundred forty-three.

Two scenes are happening at once tonight, and John cuts between them like a film editor. Inside, Jesus is being questioned by Annas, father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. Outside, in the courtyard, it's cold. Servants and officers have built a fire, and they're standing around it with their hands out. And there, among them, is Peter. Earlier tonight he said he would lay down his life for Jesus. Then he swung a sword in the garden. Now he's standing at a fire, trying to look like he belongs.

In the King James Bible: "And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself." Three times, Peter is asked. First the girl who keeps the door: "Art not thou also one of this man's disciples? He saith, I am not." Then someone at the fire asks the same thing, and again he says, I am not. Then a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter cut off: "Did not I see thee in the garden with him?" And Peter denied again, "and immediately the cock crew." Now put this beside yesterday's scene. In the garden, Jesus said, ego eimi, I am. At the fire, Peter says, ouk eimi, I am not. John sets them almost side by side. One steps forward. One steps back into the crowd. And inside, at the very same time, Jesus is telling the high priest: I spoke openly to the world; ask the people who heard me. He's naming witnesses, and one of his own disciples is outside saying he isn't one. One more detail. The Greek word for this charcoal fire is anthrakia. John will use that same word for a fire once more, much later. Hold on to that; it comes back. Readers have long found Peter's denial painful and strangely hopeful at once. It's painful because it's so ordinary: he isn't tortured, just asked by a doorkeeper. And it's hopeful because the church remembers this same Peter as a leader, later on.
screen: `A FIRE OF COALS, FOR IT WAS COLD.`
`I AM, INSIDE; I AM NOT, OUTSIDE.`
then, large: `AND PETER STOOD WITH THEM, AND WARMED HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you warm yourself. Settle, and breathe. Peter's fire was a comfort and a hiding place at the same time. Think about yours. The group you go along with. The joke you laugh at so you'll fit in. The silence you keep when someone you love isn't there to defend themselves. Don't scold yourself. Just notice, gently, where you stand to stay warm. If you pray, you can bring that place to God honestly. If you don't, simply name it to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Anthrakia. The Greek word for the charcoal fire where Peter warmed himself and said, three times, I am not.
Your line: warming himself. Today, when you catch yourself going along to stay comfortable, take one small step out of the crowd. Day six hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Peter's denial is read in churches during Holy Week, and in Christian art a rooster beside Peter recalls it, a reminder both of failure and of forgiveness.

fork.setup: you're Peter, standing at the fire. a servant girl looks at you and asks: aren't you one of his disciples? what do you say?
fork.reveal: "He saith, I am not." in the garden Jesus said 'I am'; at the fire Peter says 'I am not', three times.

original.note: Greek: a charcoal fire. John uses it here and again at 21:9.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter lied because he was scared.
what it means: at a warm fire, asked by a doorkeeper, Peter says 'I am not' three times, while inside Jesus says 'ask those who heard me'.
what a scholar hears: ego eimi in the garden and ouk eimi at the fire, and anthrakia, a word John uses here and again at 21:9.

notes: anthrakia occurs only in John 18:18 and 21:9 in the NT. Confirm.
'Annas, the old high priest': John calls him father-in-law of Caiaphas (18:13); Annas had been high priest earlier. Confirm.
Rooster on steeples as a reminder of Peter's denial: a common explanation, though weathercock origins are debated. Confirm or cut from howItsDone.
The day avoids teaching day 654's breakfast scene; it only notes the word returns.

Editor review (y2 pass): Peter says 'I am not' (one of his disciples), not that he never knew Jesus, now corrected; Annas described as 18:13 does; cut the New Testament word count for anthrakia (now: John uses it again) in voice, screen, myth, original and trapdoor; 'Christians have always' and the stock closing line cut; steeple-rooster claim (origins debated) dropped from howItsDone.
